extracted.intended_audience: researchers and PIs writing NIH grant applications / grant writers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, reviewer-focused guidance for preparing NIH grant applications (formatting, citation, and writing choices) to maximize readability and reviewer comprehension. Emphasizes making it easy for busy reviewers to scan and evaluate proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it easy for reviewers to grasp your point
rubrics_metrics.description: It is well established that approximately 85.473% of the battle when it comes to NIH Grantsmithing is making it easy for the reviewers to grasp your point. Reviewers are often overworked and will skim or scan applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the application so reviewers can quickly identify your argument and evidence. Expect reviewers to be multitasking or pressed for time (reading late at night, on a plane, with limited time). If your application is discussed and there is disagreement, non-assigned reviewers often have only ~10–15 minutes to scan the application to resolve matters. Therefore structure and clarity directly affect how well your science is apprehended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use whitespace, headings, clear figures, and direct writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Create blank space, headings, clear figures and direct writing to make the reviewer's job easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: White space is your friend — avoid dense blocks of text. Use informative headings and figure layouts that can be scanned. Edit prose for directness (avoid overly long sentences and irrelevant detail). The author repeatedly 'hammers away' at these formatting/structural elements as vital grantsmanship practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think about the reviewer audience and likely reading behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the mental image of the reviewer: overworked PI, limited attention, skimming and non-linear reading behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write and format for skimming and scanning: put key points where they are easy to find, use cues (headings, bolding when appropriate), and do not rely on reviewers reading linearly. Anticipate that many panel members will only scan the application and will not have deep familiarity with every cited paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation content requirements per NIH Application Guide
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a bibliography of any references cited in the Project Narrative. Each reference must include the names of all authors (in the same sequence in which they appear in the publication), the article and journal title, book title, volume number, page numbers, and year of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these explicit NIH bibliographic content rules. Do not reshuffle the order of co-authors. The Guide does not mandate a particular citation style (name–date vs numbered), but it requires that the pertinent bibliographic information be present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include PMCID/NIHMS identifiers for applicable publications
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing articles that fall under the Public Access Policy, were authored or co-authored by the applicant and arose from NIH support, provide the NIHMS or PMCID reference number (or indicate 'PMC Journal – In Process').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list compliance identifiers for NIH‑supported works to show adherence to public access requirements; do not omit these numbers when they apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation style matters — prefer author–date for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of citation style matters a lot. The author argues that Name, Date (author–year) citations are superior because they cue the reader to recall the cited work without flipping to the bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author–date citations often provide immediate cueing (who and when), reducing the need to consult the reference list repeatedly. This can be especially helpful when reviewers rely on their memory of specific prior findings. Use author–year when it improves comprehension and when it makes it easier to highlight your own group's work (e.g., 'PLS et al. 2011').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid numbered citations when they impede comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbered citations can make it hard for readers to figure out what work you are citing and require flipping back and forth between text and bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbered citations may save in-line space but can frustrate readers who construct arguments mentally from the citations. If you must use numbered citations (space constraints, field norms), consider using author names selectively in the narrative to emphasize key works. Be aware that many reviewers find numbered citations inferior for scanning comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not game formatting limits — edit content instead of squeezing space
rubrics_metrics.description: People who worry about 'getting more room' miss the point — the limits are there not just for the reviewer but to give the writer a sense of what is needed. If you need to push for more room, you are saying too much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cheating on margins, shrinking figures, or other layout tricks to cram more material in. Instead cut sentences or paragraphs, streamline the proposal, and focus the aims. Reviewers penalize poor presentation and cramped pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures must be legible; avoid tiny pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: Tiny pictures that reviewers can't read are a common complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure figures are large enough and clear in the PDF/printed form. High-resolution, well-labeled figures that can be quickly interpreted improve reviewer evaluation; unreadable figures reduce perceived quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good writing: avoid passive voice, typos, and sloppy English
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad writing — especially passive voice and typos — significantly irritates reviewers and reduces perceived quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for direct, active prose (the post references 'Let Hemingway be your guide'). Proofread carefully, eliminate typos, and avoid convoluted sentences. Poor writing is repeatedly listed as a top annoyance by reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full justification harms readability — avoid full-justified text
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not full-justify. It messes up word spacing and makes text harder to read and to scan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full justification can create uneven spacing and impede visual scanning; left-aligned (ragged-right) text is often more readable. Hyphenation can mitigate spacing issues for justified text, but MS Word hyphenation helps less than typesetting programs — so be cautious if you choose to justify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation and line-spacing tricks can gain space but require care
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning on hyphenation and adjusting line spacing (e.g., 11 pt Arial with line spacing set exactly to 12 pt) can free up space and look nicer, but use carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting tweaks can legitimately improve aesthetics and compactness, but they can also introduce readability problems if misused. Test PDF appearance and beware automated hyphenation errors in Word. Use allowed fonts and spacing settings consistent with NIH rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover relevant literature across the field to avoid appearing unaware
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you cite work from potentially related laboratories somewhere in the application; missing key players can create the impression the PI is 'not aware of key published findings in the field'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can't know exact review panel composition, so include citations that cover major players and relevant findings across the field. That does not mean stuffing every sentence with lengthy citation lists — place broad coverage appropriately within the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit excessive citation bloat per claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are citing 30 sources per point you are doing it wrong; more than three per claim should have a strong justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamline literature citation to those most relevant. Excessive citation density clutters the text and suggests poor focus. Use concise synthesis rather than long citation strings unless truly warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on clickable hyperlinks in PDFs for reviewer comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: While hyperlinking citations in PDFs would be convenient, reviewers are urged not to click links (possible IP concerns), so do not rely on links to supply bibliographic information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full bibliographic details in the application itself rather than depending on external links. Hyperlinks may be helpful for readers but cannot substitute for in-document clarity and required citation metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use author–date to emphasize your group's work when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Author–date citations make it easier to highlight and draw attention to work from your group (e.g., 'PLS et al. 2011').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If strategic emphasis of particular publications (your own or others') is useful for persuasion, author names in-line convey that information immediately. This can be done even in documents that otherwise use numbered citations by selectively naming authors in text.
